To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the AEPs of developmental dyslexics are characterized by an abnormally large number of components, (2) the AEP patterns of developmental dyslexia are characterized by a delay in AEPs termination time, (3) developmental dyslexics have no differential coding of voiced and voiceless consonant-vowel stimuli, (4) developmental dyslexia may involve a lack of left hemisphere specialization in auditory processing.

developmental dyslexics show anomalies of the cortical processing of time-related acoustic cues, which may be related to the presence of persistent perceptual and phonological deficits in some dyslexic adults.

the AEPs of developmental dyslexics were characterized either by a large number of components with a considerable delay in termination time, or by the lack of a clear differentiation between /ba/ (voiced) and /pa/ (voiceless) stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electrophysiological correlates of auditory processing in developmental dyslexia, a language-based learning disability affecting 5% to 10% of the population.
the study of the auditory processing of language in children with developmental language impairments, particularly in the domain of speech perception.
the electrophysiological correlates of speech processing in normal and disordered populations, and with the development of new methods to study the neural basis of language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the auditory system in developmental dyslexia has been shown to be dysfunctional, and the auditory system is a key factor in language development.

the auditory evoked potential (AEP) is a useful tool to assess the auditory system of dyslexics, and the findings of this study suggest that the AEP can be used to identify subgroups of dyslexics who may have a different underlying cause of their reading disability.
the dyslexics with the most severe reading problems have the most severe auditory processing problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the auditory system in developmental dyslexics is characterized by anomalies that may contribute to the persistent phonological deficits observed in some of them, and that the processing of time-related cues in the auditory modality may not be lateralized to the same degree as in non-dyslexically readers.
dyslexics are characterized by anomalies in cortical auditory processes that may underlie their persistent perceptual and language impairments.
the dyslexics in this study demonstrated atypical patterns of auditory evoked potentials to voiced and voice less speech sounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the processing of temporal cues that form a crucial basis for phonological processing and speech perception is atypically delayed or impaired in dyslexia.
dyslexics have a different auditory processing profile than non-dyslexia controls.
the processing of time-related cues is abnormal in dyslexic adults and that these abnormalities may be linked to persistent reading and phonological deficits in dyslexic children.
